items_missed: No agenda statement. 'I was just reaching out to conduct your kickoff call. So is this a good time?' names the purpose but gives no roadmap and no timeframe — the customer never heard that this would involve re-verifying the inventory, potentially re-quoting, and scheduling a separate video call. That matters on this call more than most, because the walkthrough ask lands out of nowhere nine minutes in and the customer's first reaction is confusion ('Sorry, so virtually').
Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up.

Packing needs never asked. A three-bedroom house with an estimated forty to fifty boxes and the question 'do you need us to pack, or will you have those ready?' was never put. On a booked move this is both a scope gap and unbilled revenue.
Additional stops never asked.

Moving-stressor question never asked. 'Do you have any questions for me in terms of the pricing or anything at all the moving process maybe?' at the very end is an invitation to ask, not a question about what worries her.
No 'pricing is super simple' opener, and no pricing framing of any kind — the rate came out only because the customer asked what it would cost.

What's-included list never given. Not gas, not the truck, not taxes, not insurance, not wrap or pads or tools. The customer is booked for a move and has never been told what the hourly rate actually buys.

Disassembly and reassembly never mentioned as included — despite Therese herself asking whether the heavy shelf comes apart ('can this [be] disassembled'). She identified the exact item that needs it and never told the customer the labor and tools are part of the rate.
Packing service pricing never given.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. No $2,000, no repair/replace/reimburse, no coverage discussion at all — on a call where the customer described her single heaviest, most awkward item and the whole move involves a steep driveway.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned.

On-Time Guarantee never mentioned — and this was the call where it mattered most. The entire opening five minutes were a negotiation about arrival windows, cycling from 8:30-9:00 to 12:30-2:30 to 9:30-10:00 because the customer wanted something closer to 11:00. She cares specifically and demonstrably about when the crew shows up, and the guarantee that Einstein discounts if it misses the window was never played.

Clock start never explained. The two-and-a-half-hour minimum never mentioned. Only the fifteen-minute proration landed ('we only charge you for the time use of the move-in fifteen minute increments'). No sense-check anywhere.

No typical time range for a three-bedroom house. She discussed four hours versus five hours purely as arithmetic against the existing quote and never told the customer what a home this size normally takes, so 'four hours' has no context and neither will whatever the walkthrough produces.

Stairs never factored. Origin is a one-story house; destination is 1,900 square feet, two stories, three bedrooms and an office downstairs — meaning most of the furniture is going up a flight. She asked about the floors and then never connected them to time or cost.
Drive time never mentioned or factored between the two Austin addresses.

Walk distance never asked or factored. She caught the steep driveway and the street-parking constraint — genuinely good probing — and then never translated it into hours, which is exactly what it costs.
Traffic never mentioned.
No equivalents or plain-language anchors used.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10. The customer handed her the opening in plain words: 'I'm familiar with how you guys work. I've moved a million times. I'll just have everything ready before you guys get here.' That is a customer volunteering to prep, asking implicitly what 'ready' means, and receiving 'Okay. Yes, ma'am. Okay, sounds good.' She is moving forty to fifty boxes out of a house with a one-car garage used as storage, down a steep driveway to a street-parked truck. Ten minutes of specifics about what to stage and what to carload would have measurably changed this move.

Nothing was sent in writing, and this is the highest-risk miss on the call. Therese moved the move date from Friday October 16th to Thursday October 15th, changed the arrival window from 8:30-9:00 to 9:30-10:00, changed the rate from $111 to $104 per mover per hour, and scheduled a virtual walkthrough for Monday October 5th at around 5:00 or 5:30 PM. Four material changes, none confirmed by email. The only thing promised in writing is a text with the walkthrough link, 'as October 5th comes closer.' No confirmation email, no bolded list of the new details, no 'reply with any corrections.' The customer hung up with a different move date than she had at the start of the call and nothing to check it against.

The walkthrough time was never actually pinned down. She asked 'what time works best for you?' and got 'After hours, I do work. So, I get like around 5:00 or 530,' and answered 'Mm-hmm okay, sure, yeah, I can definitely go ahead and do that' — then moved on. Is it 5:00 or 5:30? Neither Therese nor the customer knows, and the walkthrough is the thing this entire call exists to schedule.
Hours and how to reach us never given — 'feel free to reach back out to us' with no number and no hours.
Customer's name used zero times after the opening verification. 'Ma'am' appears roughly a dozen times and stands in for the name throughout, which reads as deferential rather than personal.

The customer's volunteered loyalty went unacknowledged. She said 'we hired you a few years ago and you all moved in very fast so you've done it before and I know you can' — an unprompted vote of confidence and a repeat-customer disclosure — and the response was 'Oh, okay. Gotcha. Let me see here.' Therese then found the 2022 record and said only 'Yes I believe this was in 2022 that you, we moved you, okay, here.' A returning customer told her she trusts the company and it drew a database lookup.

The insurance-related inventory change was noted but not resolved. The customer said 'I [have] overhead job like for insurance we have, like a couch that's on in here. We're not [taking] the put us. So, something seems we're not taking' — items are being left behind for an insurance reason — and Therese deferred the whole thing to the walkthrough rather than capturing what is out of scope now, which is the detail most likely to swing the estimate.
top_strength: Therese made the single best estimate-accuracy decision in this week's sample, and she made it against her own convenience. The customer booked online at four hours, and midway through the kickoff Therese realized the online quote never accounted for the garage or the outdoor furniture — so instead of adjusting the number on the fly the way most reps would, she stopped and routed the job to a virtual walkthrough: 'since you mentioned them that there are additional spaces that we did not take into account for when we first estimated your quote at four hours, we would usually conduct a virtual walkthrough for this. It usually takes about ten minutes just so that we can get an inventory of your home and make sure that you provide you with a more accurate estimate.' That is precisely the behavior the 52-to-80 percent estimate-accuracy work is trying to install: she recognized that the inputs were wrong, named exactly which inputs were wrong, and refused to guess. Her access probing is also the most thorough of the eight calls and it is the kind that actually costs crews time when missed. She asked about the garage, then whether it's one or two car, then whether a car still fits or whether it's being used as storage — three layered questions to size an unseen load. She asked about truck parking at both addresses ('do you have a driveway that we can use to park the truck or should we park along the [street]') and the customer volunteered the constraint that will shape the whole load-out: 'Along the [street], just a heads-up. The driveway is a very steep driveway.' And she asked the special-considerations question in the specific, concrete form the rubric wants, which nobody else did: 'any other special considerations in terms of access to either home, low hanging branches [tight] turns or [tight] hallways or anything like that.' She also handled the arrival window with real patience — the customer wanted something around 11:00, Therese offered both standard windows, absorbed the pushback, went and found a middle option ('the latest that we can do in the morning would be a 9:30 AM to 10:00 AM start window'), and landed it. Then, entirely unprompted, she surfaced the cheaper day tier and turned it into money in the customer's pocket: 'it is $111 per hour per mover on that Friday which is a standard [rate] day. We typically have lower rates on Tuesday to Thursday,' and when the customer bit, she quantified it and executed immediately — 'if we move you on say the fifteenth, the rate would go down from $111 to $104 per hour' and 'I can definitely move your booking to Thursday the 15th of October.' Correct per-mover-per-hour framing, a proactive saving the customer never asked for, and the booking change made on the call.
coaching_note: Classified as walkthrough_scheduler: this is a kickoff on an already-booked online reservation that Therese correctly routes to a virtual walkthrough because the original inventory was incomplete. Per the rubric, the pricing, clock, estimate and Save Your Ass sections do not cleanly apply on a walkthrough intake — the full estimate is deliberately deferred to October 5th. I have still scored all nine sections against the 85-point rubric as instructed, so the low pricing and clock numbers here reflect a call structure that was partly correct by design, and the score should not be read against a full sales call one-for-one. The exception, and it is the one to coach: this customer is already booked. She has a date, a window, a rate, and a crew coming to her house. Deferring the estimate is right; deferring the clock mechanics, the what's-included list, and the three differentiators is not, because there may be no other call before move day. She does not know there is a two-and-a-half-hour minimum. She does not know when the clock starts. She does not know what the $104 an hour buys, that disassembly is included, or that there is up to two thousand dollars of damage coverage on a move where her heaviest shelf goes down a steep driveway. Every one of those belongs on a kickoff call whether or not a walkthrough is happening. The On-Time Guarantee in particular was the layup she missed: five minutes of this call were spent negotiating arrival windows, so the customer has told you unambiguously that timing is what she cares about. 'And one more thing on the window — we guarantee it. If we show up outside your 9:30 to 10:00, we start discounting the move immediately.' Highest-leverage fix overall, though, is that nothing went in writing. Therese changed this customer's move date, her arrival window, and her hourly rate, and scheduled a video call, and sent no confirmation email. The only promised written contact is a text with the walkthrough link 'as October 5th comes closer.' If the customer misremembers Thursday as Friday, or shows up expecting 8:30, there is no artifact to check. The close should have been: 'I'm sending your updated confirmation now — the new date, Thursday October 15th, your 9:30 to 10:00 window, the $104 per mover rate, and the walkthrough on Monday the 5th are all bolded at the top. Give those a read and reply if anything's off.' That is the email handoff bullet, and it is also basic operational hygiene on a call where four things changed. Pin the walkthrough time while you are at it — '5:00 or 5:30' is not a calendar entry, and the walkthrough is the entire point of the call. Second, the Save Your Ass speech was declined when the customer offered it to her. 'I'll just have everything ready before you guys get here' is a prompt, and it got 'Okay, sounds good.' A customer with forty to fifty boxes, a storage garage, and a steep driveway asking what 'ready' means is the best possible audience for 'stage everything by the garage door, consolidate the loose stuff in drawers and closets, and anything small enough to carry, take a carload over yourself — all of it comes off the clock.' Ten points on the scorecard and real hours off a move she is already paying for. Third, and smallest but worth naming: a repeat customer told her 'we hired you a few years ago and you all moved in very fast so you've done it before and I know you can,' and it drew a lookup rather than a thank you. 'That means a lot — and honestly that's the best kind of feedback we get. Let me make sure this one goes just as smoothly' costs nothing and is the difference between a vendor and a company she recommends.
phone_presence_notes: Patient, polite and genuinely accommodating on the arrival-window negotiation, and the proactive move to the cheaper Thursday rate showed she was working on the customer's behalf — but the warmth stayed formal rather than personal: roughly a dozen 'ma'am's stand in for the customer's name, which was never used once, the delivery leans on 'alright / okay / gotcha' as connective filler, and the customer's unprompted expression of trust ('I know you can') was answered with 'Oh, okay. Gotcha. Let me see here.'
